items.text: In 2019, it comprised three tasks: (1A) identifying relationships between citing documents and the referred document, (1B) classifying the discourse facets, and (2) generating the abstractive summary.
items.why: Defines the three tasks comprising the CL-SciSumm shared task.
items.plain: In 2019, the challenge included three tasks: Task 1A connects cited and citing papers, Task 1B categorizes the type of scientific discourse, and Task 2 creates an abstract-style summary.

items.text: The dataset comprised 40 annotated sets of citing and reference papers of the CL-SciSumm 2018 corpus and 1000 more from the SciSumm- Net dataset.
items.why: Specifies dataset sources and counts used in the shared task.
items.plain: The dataset contains 40 annotated paper sets from the CL-SciSumm 2018 corpus and 1,000 additional sets from SciSumm-Net.

items.text: Given: A topic consists of a Reference Paper (RP) and ten or more Citing Papers (CPs) that all contain citations to the RP.
items.why: Defines the input topic composition consisting of reference and citing papers.
items.plain: A single topic includes one reference paper and at least ten citing papers that cite it.

items.text: – the abstract, written by the authors of the research paper. – the community summary, collated from the reference spans of its citances. – a human-written summary, written by the annotators of the CL-SciSumm
items.why: Defines the three summary types provided in the dataset for reference papers.
items.plain: The dataset includes three summaries per reference paper: the author abstract, a community summary made from cited passages, and a summary written by human annotators.

items.text: Task 1A: For each citance, identify the spans of text (cited text spans) in the RP that most accurately reﬂect the citance.
items.why: Defines the objective for Task 1A.
items.plain: For Task 1A, systems must locate the specific text passages in the reference paper that best match each citation sentence.

items.text: These are of the granularity of a sentence fragment, a full sentence, or several consecutive sentences (no more than 5).
items.why: Specifies the granularity constraints for text spans in Task 1A.
items.plain: The target text spans can be a sentence fragment, a full sentence, or up to 5 consecutive sentences.

items.text: Task 1B: For each cited text span, identify what facet of the paper it belongs to, from a predeﬁned set of facets.
items.why: Defines the objective for Task 1B.
items.plain: For Task 1B, systems must classify each chosen reference passage into a predefined discourse category.

items.text: Task 2: Finally, generate a structured summary of the RP from the cited text spans of the RP.
items.why: Defines the objective for Task 2.
items.plain: For Task 2, systems must generate a structured summary of the reference paper using its cited text passages.

items.text: The length of the summary should not exceed 250 words.
items.why: States the maximum word limit for Task 2 generated summaries.
items.plain: Generated summaries must not exceed 250 words.

items.text: Speciﬁcally, for Task 1, we used the method proposed by [17] to prepare noisy training data for about 1000 unannotated papers.
items.why: Explains how noisy training data was generated for Task 1.
items.plain: For Task 1, roughly 1000 unannotated papers were automatically processed to create noisy training data.

items.text: This method involves automatically matching a citance in a CP with approximately similar reference spans in its RPs.
items.why: Describes the automated matching mechanism for generating Task 1 training data.
items.plain: This method automatically matches citation sentences in citing papers to similar passages in the referenced paper.

items.text: For Task 1A, they use multi-classiﬁers and integrate their results via voting system.
items.why: Describes System 1's approach to Task 1A using multi-classifiers and voting.
items.plain: System 1 uses multiple classification models for Task 1A and combines their results using a voting system.

items.text: Compared with previous work, this year they make new selection of features based on correlation analysis, apply similarity-based negative sampling strategy when creating training dataset and add deep learning models for classiﬁcations.
items.why: Details System 1's feature selection, negative sampling, and classification models.
items.plain: System 1 selected features using correlation analysis, created training data via similarity-based negative sampling, and added deep learning models.

items.text: In order to improve the performance of summarization, they develop more semantic representations for sentences based on neural network language models to construct new kernel matrix used in Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs).
items.why: Explains System 2's approach to Task 2 using neural language models and DPPs.
items.plain: To improve summarization, System 2 used neural network language models to represent sentence meaning and build kernel matrices for Determinantal Point Processes.

items.text: They explored the potential of ﬁnetuning bidirectional transformers for the identiﬁcation of cited passages.
items.why: Describes System 3's use of fine-tuned bidirectional transformers for Task 1.
items.plain: System 3 fine-tuned bidirectional transformer language models to locate cited passages.

items.text: They further formalised the task as a similarity ranking problem and implemented bilateral multi-perspective matching for natural language sentences.
items.why: Details System 3's ranking framework using bilateral multi-perspective matching.
items.plain: System 3 framed Task 1 as a ranking problem and used bilateral multi-perspective matching to compare sentences.

items.text: They ﬁrst identify candidate sentences in the reference paper and compute their similarities to the citing sentence using tf-idf and embedding-based methods as well as other features such as POS tags.
items.why: Describes System 4's candidate selection using tf-idf, embeddings, and POS tags.
items.plain: System 4 found target sentences by measuring text similarity using tf-idf, word embeddings, and part-of-speech tags.

items.text: In particular, for task 1A, they locate the related text spans referred to by the citation text by creating paired text representations and employ pre-trained embedding mechanisms in conjunction with XGBoost, a gradient boosted decision tree algorithm to identify textual entailment.
items.why: Details System 7's Task 1A pipeline using paired representations, embeddings, and XGBoost.
items.plain: System 7 represented sentence pairs using pre-trained embeddings and classified textual entailment using the XGBoost decision tree algorithm.

items.text: They propose a supervised system based on recurrent neural networks and an unsupervised system based on sentence similarity for Task 1A, one supervised approach for Task 1B, and one supervised approach for Task 2.
items.why: Outlines System 8's architecture for Tasks 1A, 1B, and 2.
items.plain: System 8 used recurrent neural networks and sentence similarity for Task 1A, and supervised models for Tasks 1B and 2.

items.text: Facet assignment is based on the relative positions of the cited sentences locally to the corresponding section and globally in the entire paper.
items.why: Explains System 9's local and global position features for facet assignment.
items.plain: System 9 assigned facets based on where cited sentences appeared within their specific section and within the entire paper.

items.text: Task 2 is addressed by predicting the overlap (in terms of units of text) between the selected text spans and the summary generated by the domain experts.
items.why: Describes System 9's Task 2 objective of predicting overlap with expert summaries.
items.plain: System 9 performed Task 2 by predicting how much text overlap selected candidate sentences would have with human expert summaries.

items.text: They propose a novel listwise ranking method for cited text identiﬁcation.
items.why: Introduces System 12's listwise ranking approach for cited text identification.
items.plain: System 12 used a listwise ranking method to identify cited text passages.

items.text: Their method have two stages: similarity-based ranking and supervised listwise ranking.
items.why: Outlines the two stages of System 12's ranking framework.
items.plain: System 12's method consists of a similarity-based ranking step followed by a supervised listwise ranking step.

items.text: In the ﬁrst stage, we select the top-5 sentences per a citation text, due to the modiﬁed Jaccard similarity.
items.why: Describes System 12's first-stage candidate filtering using modified Jaccard similarity.
items.plain: In the first stage, System 12 selected the top 5 candidate sentences per citation using a modified Jaccard similarity metric.

items.text: These top-5 selected sentences are proceeded to rank by a CitedListNet (listwise ranking model based on deep learning).
items.why: Explains System 12's second-stage deep learning model CitedListNet.
items.plain: In the second stage, System 12 ranked the top 5 sentences using a deep learning model called CitedListNet.

items.text: They use sentences from selected zones to ﬁnd the most similar ones of the rest sentences of the paper which constitute the “candidate sentences”.
items.why: Explains System 17's candidate sentence retrieval method via abstract zone similarity.
items.plain: System 17 selected candidate sentences from the paper by finding those most similar to sentences in specific abstract zones.

items.text: Secondly, they employ a siamese bi-directional GRU neural network with a logistic regression layer to classify if a citation sentence cites a candidate sentence.
items.why: Details System 17's siamese GRU model for citation link classification.
items.plain: System 17 used a siamese bidirectional GRU neural network with logistic regression to determine if a citation referenced a candidate sentence.

items.text: An automatic evaluation script was used to measure system performance for Task 1A, in terms of the sentence ID overlaps between the sentences identiﬁed in system output, versus the gold standard created by human annotators.
items.why: Explains evaluation protocol for Task 1A using sentence ID overlap.
items.plain: Task 1A performance was evaluated by checking sentence ID overlaps between predicted sentences and human annotations.

items.text: The raw number of overlapping sentences were used to calculate the precision, recall and F1 score for each system.
items.why: States the core evaluation metrics used for Task 1A.
items.plain: Precision, recall, and F1 score were calculated based on the count of overlapping sentences.

items.text: Additionally, we calculated lexical overlaps in terms of the ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-SU4 scores [11] between the system output and the human annotated gold standard reference spans.
items.why: Describes lexical overlap evaluation for Task 1A using ROUGE metrics.
items.plain: Task 1A was also evaluated by measuring ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-SU4 word overlap between predictions and target text spans.

items.text: Task 1B was evaluated as a proportion of the correctly classiﬁed discourse facets by the system, contingent on the expected response of Task 1A.
items.why: Explains Task 1B evaluation dependency on Task 1A identification correctness.
items.plain: Task 1B was evaluated by calculating the proportion of correctly classified facets, contingent on correct sentence identification in Task 1A.

items.text: Task 2 was optional, and also evaluated using the ROUGE–2 and ROUGE– SU4 scores between the system output and three types of gold standard summaries of the research paper: the reference paper’s abstract, a community summary, and a human summary.
items.why: Details Task 2 evaluation protocol against three summary reference types.
items.plain: Task 2 was evaluated using ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-SU4 against abstracts, community summaries, and human-written summaries.

items.text: For Task 1A, the best performance was shown by System 3 (Team UoM) [24].
items.why: States the top performing system for Task 1A.
items.plain: System 3 achieved the highest performance in Task 1A.

items.text: The third best system was system 2 (Team CIST-BUPT) which was also the best performer for Task 1B, the classiﬁcation task.
items.why: States the top performing system for Task 1B.
items.plain: System 2 ranked third in Task 1A and achieved the best performance for Task 1B facet classification.

items.text: On the summarisation task, Task 2, System 3 (Team UoM) had the best performance against the abstract.
items.why: States the best Task 2 system when evaluated against abstracts.
items.plain: System 3 achieved the best Task 2 performance when evaluated against paper abstracts.

items.text: System 2 (Team CIST-BUPT) had the best performance for community and human summaries.
items.why: States the best Task 2 system against community and human summaries.
items.plain: System 2 achieved the highest Task 2 scores against community and human-written summaries.

items.text: The best Task 1a performance (sentence overlap F1) this year is 0.126 from System 3 [24] which is a deep learning system trained on augmented data.
items.why: Reports the top Task 1A F1 score and winning system.
items.plain: System 3 won Task 1A with a sentence overlap F1 score of 0.126 using a deep learning model trained on expanded data.

items.text: The best on CL-SciSumm ’19 Task 2 performance on human written summaries on ROUGE-2 is 0.278 by [10].
items.why: Reports the top Task 2 ROUGE-2 score against human summaries.
items.plain: System 2 achieved the top Task 2 ROUGE-2 score of 0.278 against human-written summaries.

items.text: This implies that for Task 1a, traditional models trained on clean data perform better than deep learning models trained on noisy data.
items.why: Presents comparative finding regarding model performance on clean vs noisy data.
items.plain: For Task 1A, traditional machine learning models trained on clean data outperformed deep learning models trained on noisy data.

items.text: However, if we look at CL-SciSumm ’19 systems’ performances, we notice that deep learning models perform better than traditional machine learning models when trained on the augmented data.
items.why: Presents finding on deep learning models trained on augmented data.
items.plain: When trained on augmented data, deep learning models outperformed traditional machine learning models in 2019.

items.text: On Task 1b, systems using traditional methods perform better than deep learning systems.
items.why: Notes that traditional methods outperformed deep learning for Task 1B.
items.plain: Traditional machine learning approaches achieved better results than deep learning approaches on Task 1B.

items.text: On Task 2, the best performing system on human summaries, System 2, using neural representations trained on the 1000 plus summaries, does the best with a ROUGE-2 score of 0.278.
items.why: Reports winning Task 2 neural model results on human summaries.
items.plain: On Task 2, System 2 used neural representations trained on over 1000 summaries to achieve the top ROUGE-2 score of 0.278 on human summaries.

items.text: With a score of 0.514 System 3 also improves the state-of-the-art agasint abstracts by 0.2 on ROUGE-2 score.
items.why: Reports System 3's benchmark result on ROUGE-2 against abstracts.
items.plain: System 3 achieved a ROUGE-2 score of 0.514 against paper abstracts, improving the state of the art by 0.2.

items.text: System 3 is also the top system on community summaries with a ROUGE-2 score of 0.204.
items.why: Reports System 3's top score on community summaries.
items.plain: System 3 achieved the highest ROUGE-2 score of 0.204 on community summaries.
